Grounded instruction proposal.

To avoid repeatedly covering familiar functionality, we maintain global application memory that records functions previously exercised for each application and expose it during subsequent exploration. When additional interface information is needed, the Exploration Agent may perform a short non-destructive inspection using only open, click, scroll, and done. Keyboard and free-form text input are unavailable to avoid mutating the known initial state. It then proposes a goal-oriented instruction and fine-grained success conditions for evaluator synthesis. The resulting instruction record contains fields such as snapshot, versioned related_apps, instruction, config, complexity, category, success_criteria, and evaluation_requirements_text. The instruction field is the core user-facing task specification. The snapshot, related_apps, and config fields are determined during initialization and record the reproducible environment context. The category field is generated by the Exploration Agent together with the instruction and is divided into three groups. app_only denotes tasks centered on application or system functionality, such as changing software or user settings. file_only denotes tasks centered on processing input files whose final deliverables are file artifacts. mixed denotes tasks that involve both. The complexity field estimates the length of a pure-GUI solution. We label tasks with 5–15 steps as easy, tasks with 15–40 steps as medium, and tasks with more than 40 steps as complex. The success_criteria field lists the terminal conditions that must hold after successful task completion. The evaluation_requirements_text field translates those conditions into concrete checks for evaluator synthesis, such as which file, slide, field, format, or application state should be inspected. The instruction states non-answer constraints such as locations, scope, ordering, quantity, format, and filenames. Exact observed values are retained only in these hidden success and evaluation fields.

Evaluator synthesis.

Evaluator synthesis begins only after an instruction proposal has been accepted and is performed by an independent Evaluator Agent in a separate context. Its inputs are the frozen instruction fields, initialization configuration, success criteria, and textual evaluation requirements. The Evaluator Agent may generate only the verification specification and cannot revise the instruction or proposal metadata. A rule-based evaluator comprises one or more self-contained Python judge functions. Each function declares its required imports locally, can run independently, accepts result and expected as inputs, and typically evaluates one well-defined subgoal. Either input may be supplied by vm_file as a VM-resident file or by vm_command_line as command-observable state. When initialization creates a local golden copy, expected may refer to it for content or structural comparison. When the target can be encoded directly in the rule, expected may be empty. Each judge accumulates a rubric-based score over fine-grained completion items with assigned weights. It returns a value in [0,1][0,1], with zero for no satisfied items and one for complete satisfaction; if execution raises an exception, it returns the score accumulated before the exception. The evaluator relies only on VM-resident artifacts and deterministic rules, without external or cloud-hosted golden assets, and checks the final artifact’s content, structure, formatting, metadata, or configuration state.

When deterministic rules fully express the success conditions, the evaluator sets need_rule_judge=true without enabling visual judgment. When visual layout, canvas state, unparsable application-internal state, or dynamic web content is indispensable for verification, it may set need_vlm_judge=true. In this case, the VLM judge receives the agent’s execution trajectory as input, and vlm_desc specifies the visual objects, attributes, and spatial relations to inspect in that trajectory.

Rule-based and VLM-based judgments may both be used for task verification, but their scores are recorded separately. For a task with multiple rule judges, the rule-based score is the mean of the individual rule-judge scores, whereas the VLM-based score is produced independently by visual judgment. During SFT filtering, the two scores are thresholded separately, and a task is retained only when both its rule-based score and VLM-based score meet their respective thresholds (both 0.8). As described in Section 4.1, RL uses only tasks with rule-based evaluators to provide reward signals. This design avoids the brittleness and computational cost of VLM judgment and prevents the calibration mismatch that could arise from averaging the two score types directly. Although both scores lie in [0,1][0,1], rule-based scores are derived from fine-grained, explicitly weighted completion items, whereas VLM scores generally reflect a coarser and more subjective judgment scale. The two scores therefore do not have interchangeable numerical semantics. Consequently, VLM judgment is used primarily to cover programmatic observability gaps during SFT-stage filtering.

Instruction and evaluator filtering.

Filtering first checks whether the JSON schema, getter arguments, and Python code can be parsed and compiled statically. The system then initializes the environment from the initialization configuration and executes the evaluator before any action. The initial-state score must be zero, as a nonzero score indicates reward leakage. An independent review model next scores instruction quality and evaluator quality separately. The former assesses whether the instruction is unambiguous, reachable, and realistic, while the latter assesses whether the evaluator covers all success conditions, is sufficiently strict, and resists reward hacking. An instruction below the quality threshold is removed directly. If the instruction is valid but its evaluator fails an automated check or quality review, the system uses the previous evaluator and its failure information as revision context, regenerates the evaluator, and repeats the full validation and scoring procedure. The associated proposal is removed only after multiple repair attempts remain unsuccessful.

After correctness filtering, we use embedding similarity to remove near-duplicate instructions generated across batches, producing the task pool used for training stages. The RL task pool is then built by rolling out trajectories with the SFT-trained model on this pool and keeping tasks of moderate difficulty.

Prototype cross-application extension.

Beyond the application–system compositions in the primary task pool, we implemented and began collecting a more structured form of cross-application task synthesis. The prototype uses the related_app field in the application configurations to construct an application graph. Applications serve as nodes, while edges encode compositional relations induced by shared artifact types or file formats, convertible intermediate artifacts, or complementary workflows. This graph provides a structured prior for composing applications rather than treating all application combinations as equally plausible. For each task, the system first specifies a target number of applications, such as three, randomly samples a primary application, and then samples subsequent applications from its neighboring nodes. After each selection, the neighbors of the selected nodes are added to the candidate frontier, allowing the application set to expand along graph structure. To prevent the graph from overly constraining the composition space, each sampling step retains a small-probability jump mechanism that ignores graph connectivity and samples an application uniformly from the broader inventory. Artifact selection follows a corresponding compositional procedure and may introduce zero or more related artifacts. This setting expands the exploration space and requires the Exploration Agent to additionally infer cross-application dependencies, including the execution order and the transfer of artifacts or intermediate results, before proposing a long-horizon instruction.

We have already generated a small number of such prototype tasks and included them in the task pool. Their current scale is insufficient for a systematic evaluation of cross-application capabilities, so future work will expand the collection and study its effect on long-horizon execution across applications.

B.5 Instruction and Action Distributions

Figure 5 summarizes the synthesized tasks and desktop SFT data from four complementary perspectives. Panel (a) groups the 8,880 tasks generated before filtering by application domain. Panel (b) reports the task-level evaluator composition over all 8,880 generated tasks, distinguishing rule-only, VLM-only, and hybrid rule–VLM evaluation. Panel (c) partitions the full pool of 83,701 desktop SFT samples, collected from trajectories for 5,416 tasks after filtering, including successful samples, failed samples, and three invalid-sample categories covering tool-call format or schema errors, content-quality issues, and other issues. Panel (d) shows the distribution of 40,729 tool actions in the successful SFT samples.

B.6 General Data Mixture

The SFT data mixture follows a commonly used roughly 1:1 mixing ratio, consisting of approximately 31K filtered distilled desktop samples and 40K general-purpose samples. The general-purpose data covers GUI understanding, coding, mathematics, OCR, chart interpretation, and dialogue, helping stabilize model training and reduce over-specialization to desktop trajectories.

Appendix C Training Details

C.1 SFT Configuration

We perform full-parameter SFT with Megatron-SWIFT (Zhao et al., 2025). Training uses tensor parallelism of 4, pipeline parallelism of 1, and bfloat16 precision. We set the global and micro batch sizes to 16 and 1, respectively, train for one epoch, use a maximum sequence length of 32,768, and enable sample packing. The learning rate is 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}, with a minimum learning rate of 1×10−61\times 10^{-6} and a warmup fraction of 0.05. In addition to the settings in Table 10, we enable full recomputation, FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022), FlashLinearAttention (Yang and Zhang, 2024), and sequence parallelism for efficient and stable long-context full-parameter training.

C.2 GSPO RL Configuration

Our RL system is built on the asynchronous Slime framework (Zhu et al., 2025), augmented with custom training logic for online desktop interaction. Each rollout collection contains 8 prompts and samples 8 trajectories per prompt, yielding 64 rollout samples per collection. We use a maximum of 50 GUI interaction steps, a rollout temperature of 0.5, and a maximum response length of 10,240. Tasks are dynamically sampled according to an exponential moving average of their success rates. SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) serves as the rollout backend, while Megatron (Shoeybi et al., 2019) is used for policy training. The RL objective is Step-balanced GSPO, with disabled KL divergence and equal weights of 1.0 for GUI and code steps. The full configuration is listed in Table 11.

C.3 Online RL Sampling, Segmentation, and Rewards

Uniform task sampling is inefficient for online CUA training because many rollouts are spent on tasks that are either already solved or still out of reach. Following the frontier-sampling intuition in prior ScaleCUA (Lv et al., 2026), we maintain a success-rate estimate for each task and bias sampling toward tasks near the current capability frontier.

For each task ii, we initialize p^i=0.5\hat{p}_{i}=0.5. After each update window, if nin_{i} new rollouts are available for task ii, we update its success-rate estimate by

p^i←αp^i+(1−α)⋅1ni∑j=1ni𝟏[ri,j>0],\hat{p}_{i}\leftarrow\alpha\hat{p}_{i}+(1-\alpha)\cdot\frac{1}{n_{i}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{i}}\mathbf{1}[r_{i,j}>0],

where α\alpha is the EMA retention coefficient, consistent with the task-sampling EMA parameter in Table 11. The task sampling weight is then computed with a Gaussian kernel,

wi=exp⁡(−(p^i−μ)22​σ2),w_{i}=\exp\left(-\frac{(\hat{p}_{i}-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right),

We set the target success rate to μ=0.5\mu=0.5 and the bandwidth to σ=0.25\sigma=0.25. Thus tasks with very high or very low estimated success rates receive lower weights, while tasks near the target success rate are sampled more often.

To control visual-context length, we use a bounded sliding-window strategy. Each rollout maintains a history of 5–10 screenshots. When the history exceeds 10 screenshots, we save the current stream as a training segment, discard the five oldest screenshots, retain the five most recent screenshots, and resume collecting observations. Only assistant responses generated while the retained screenshot history lies in this 5–10 range contribute to the loss. Earlier context tokens are retained only as conditioning information with loss mask 00.

Rewards come only from the paired environment evaluator, env.evaluate. We do not use auxiliary format rewards or handcrafted step-level rewards. For valid trajectories and segments, evaluator scores are real values in [0,1][0,1]. If an assistant response contains an unparsable tool call, an action outside the allowed schema, or another invalid action-format failure, that response is extracted as a separate invalid sample and assigned reward 00, even if the remaining trajectory could otherwise obtain a positive task-level score. This prevents malformed actions from receiving accidental positive credit through later recovery.

Appendix D Extra Experiments

D.1 Transfer to WindowsAgentArena

Table 12 reports additional results for the 27B backbone and its corresponding OS-Helix variants on WindowsAgentArena, providing evidence of transfer from the Ubuntu-based training setting to this Windows benchmark. We retain the GUI and Hybrid baselines from the main experiments to preserve the same comparison between action-space access and learned hybrid behavior. Of particular note, since the operating system environment is Windows, we restrict Code actions to Python only, excluding the use of Bash. When Cmd/PowerShell commands would otherwise be required, system calls are instead issued directly within Python; this adaptation is implemented via prompt revision.

Despite the absence of Windows-specific training data, OS-Helix improves on this benchmark. The SFT-only OS-Helix-27B raises the matched GUI backbone from 40.82% to 57.95%, a gain of 17.13 absolute points, and the RL variant reaches 63.87%, exceeding the GUI baseline by 23.05 points and the Hybrid baseline by 7.46 points. The unadapted Hybrid baseline also improves substantially over GUI (56.41% versus 40.82%), while OS-Helix-27B adds a further 1.54 points. These comparisons provide benchmark-specific evidence that learned GUI/code routing transfers to WindowsAgentArena under the reported Python-only prompt adaptation.

The remaining gap is also diagnostic. Manual inspection of failed WindowsAgentArena trajectories shows that OS-Helix-27B often identifies the correct high-level strategy but can fail in the concrete system-command layer, mixing Bash-like patterns into Windows execution or producing brittle PowerShell-style logic despite the Python-only prompt adaptation. This pattern is compatible with the absence of Windows-specific command data. In contextual comparisons reported on the same benchmark, OS-Helix-27B-RL slightly exceeds OS-Symphony w/ GPT-5 and Agent S3 w/ GPT-5 under the shared 50-step budget. These results motivate scaling the synthesis pipeline along the operating-system dimension and evaluating on broader Windows and macOS task distributions.

We further analyze infeasible tasks as a complementary limitation of the current data pipeline. Both OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena contain a non-negligible fraction of infeasible tasks, roughly 10% of their task sets. These tasks mix at least two phenomena: genuinely impossible instructions whose target condition cannot be satisfied, and GUI-infeasible tasks where the visual route may be blocked while a programmatic route could still modify the underlying state. Our synthesis pipeline is designed around executable goal states and therefore does not naturally generate infeasible training tasks. As a result, the model can under-learn when to stop and declare infeasibility, often continuing until the maximum interaction budget is exhausted. Conversely, for tasks that are infeasible only under GUI interaction, a hybrid agent may legitimately solve them through code, which can still be judged as incorrect if the benchmark expects infeasibility recognition. As a diagnostic, after removing infeasible tasks from the evaluation set, the average success rate on OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena increases by up to 3–5 absolute points. This suggests that future task design and data synthesis should explicitly model infeasibility, distinguishing true task impossibility from modality-specific infeasibility so that agents can learn both effective execution and calibrated refusal.

D.2 Additional Analysis

The diagnostic experiments in this subsection are conducted with Qwen3-series models (Bai et al., 2025), which differ from the Qwen3.5-series base models used in the experiments above. The training data and data recipe, however, are kept exactly the same, so the comparison isolates how the same OS-Helix training signal behaves on a different backbone family.

All experiments in this subsection use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) only and do not include reinforcement learning (RL). Accordingly, the analyses below study the transferability of the learned GUI/code behavior and the information content of the SFT data, rather than the contribution of online policy optimization.

D.2.1 Grounding Ability Check

Table 13 reports grounding benchmark performance on Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct and an OS-Helix-32B variant with the same data recipe as our Qwen3.5-series models. The reproduced base model obtains 61.35 on OSWorld-G (Xie et al., 2026) and 95.05 on ScreenSpot-V2 (Wu et al., 2025), while OS-Helix-32B obtains 57.21 and 93.47, respectively.

This decrease is expected rather than contradictory to our main results. The training objective does not only optimize pixel grounding; it also teaches the model to format tool calls, reason over files, invoke code when programmatic execution is more reliable, and recover from multi-step environment feedback. In this sense, the model reallocates some capacity away from isolated grounding benchmarks toward hybrid desktop execution. The key observation is that even when pure grounding slightly decreases, code-capable action selection can compensate for this loss in end-to-end tasks by avoiding brittle pixel-level interactions and solving precise file or data operations through the operating system.

D.2.2 Backbone Replacement Analysis

To test whether the training signal transfers beyond the original backbone, we repeat the SFT experiment with Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking. Table 14 reports the complete OSWorld breakdown; arrows in the OS-Helix rows denote absolute-point changes relative to the Qwen3-VL baseline under the same Setting. With the Instruct backbone, adding Code without training a hybrid policy slightly decreases the baseline from 34.17% (GUI) to 32.68% (Hybrid). After SFT, however, OS-Helix-32B reaches 50.56%, a +17.88-point improvement over the matched Hybrid baseline. With the Thinking backbone, the unadapted Hybrid baseline is somewhat better than GUI (42.88% versus 39.08%), but OS-Helix-32B-Thinking still improves it by +8.79 points to 51.67%. Thus, the result isolates two effects: Code availability is not itself sufficient for reliable hybrid execution, while the SFT training signal transfers across both backbones and converts the available action space into a substantially stronger policy.

The domain-level changes clarify what is learned. For Instruct, OS-Helix-32B improves all five domains over the matched Hybrid baseline. The corresponding gains in OS, Office, Daily, Prof., and Work. are 16.67, 19.66, 16.83, 12.24, and 19.76 points, respectively. The gains are therefore broad rather than being explained by a single application family, with the largest improvements in Office and multi-application tasks in the Work. category. This pattern is consistent with learning cross-step state management and modality routing, rather than simply improving visual grounding on isolated screens. For Thinking, the gains remain broad in OS (+8.33), Office (+11.94), Daily (+11.40), and Work. (+9.40), but Prof. decreases by 2.83 points. The single negative domain is a useful qualification: backbone replacement does not erase model-specific priors, and SFT can redistribute capability unevenly across application families. Nevertheless, the positive average and the gains across the OS, Office, Daily, and Work. categories show that the central hybrid behavior is not tied to one backbone’s pretrained tool-use bias.

These results also strengthen the distinction between action-space access and policy learning in the main claim. The Instruct baseline provides a controlled counterexample in which the same model becomes slightly worse when Code is merely exposed at inference time. In contrast, the trained model gains most strongly on domains where successful execution requires coordinating GUI observations, executable operations, and persistent task state. The improvement should therefore be interpreted as evidence for learned coordination and routing, not as an artifact of giving the model an additional tool.

D.2.3 Training Recipe and Context Analysis

We next isolate how the structure of demonstrations and test-time history affects performance, using Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct with OSWorld. The normal recipe reaches 50.56%. Removing CoT from training and retaining actions only reduces performance to 37.74% (-12.82 points), while keeping the training data unchanged but removing CoT from the inference context yields 37.82% (-12.74 points). The near-identical degradation is important: the reasoning trace is not merely an auxiliary training target. It also functions as an execution-time state representation that helps the model maintain intent, resolve intermediate observations, and select between GUI and code actions across multi-step execution.

Removing only historical CoT is less damaging, but still lowers the average to 43.22% (-7.34 points). This partial recovery indicates that the current-step decision can retain useful local information, yet removing the accumulated reasoning history weakens temporal credit assignment and state tracking. The effect is especially visible in the Work. category, where success falls from 38.54% to 28.87% without training CoT, 31.43% without inference CoT, and 31.30% without historical CoT. Multi-application tasks therefore expose the central role of structured context most clearly: their difficulty lies not only in individual grounding decisions, but in preserving a coherent plan while the active application and tool modality change.

Finally, mixing in trajectories rejected during filtering reduces the score to 47.06% (-3.50 points). This smaller but consistent decline suggests that data quality is not interchangeable with data quantity. Rejected failures may preserve superficial action patterns, but they also introduce inconsistent or non-executable supervision that blurs the association between observations, tool calls, and successful state transitions. Taken together, the ablations support a precise interpretation of the SFT recipe: CoT and history provide the structured latent state needed for hybrid execution, while rejection filtering protects the reliability of the behavior-to-outcome mapping. The full comparison is given in Table 15.

Appendix E Step-Balanced GSPO Details

During reinforcement learning, a training sample may contain multiple assistant responses that contribute to the policy loss, with each response corresponding to one action step. The optimization unit of a training sample therefore need not coincide with an individual environment action step. In particular, the assistant span associated with a code action step is often substantially longer than that associated with a GUI step. The standard GSPO objective computes one sample-level importance ratio by aggregating token-level log-importance weights over all valid assistant tokens in the training sample (Zheng et al., 2025). Although this prevents a sample from receiving a larger sample-level weight solely because it contains more tokens, it does not equalize the contributions of different action steps within the same sample. As a result, a long code action can dominate both the sample-level ratio and the clipping decision even when it is only one of several actions in the training sample.

This section formalizes the effect and derives a step-balanced aggregation for the GSPO ratio. Our goal is to preserve GSPO’s token-level importance weights and clipping structure while changing their sample-level aggregation to remove the deterministic dependence of an action step’s aggregate gradient coefficient on its token count. Recent work has also studied the granularity of importance ratios for LLM policy optimization, including sequence-level GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025), subsentence-level ratios (Yang et al., 2025a), cumulative token ratios (Zhang et al., 2026b), and hybrid token/sequence ratios (Min et al., 2026). These methods differ from our setting at the objective level. SSPO assigns separate ratios to text fragments, but its published objective aggregates fragments with token-length normalization and does not use environment-action boundaries or action-type weights. CTPO and DHPO use token-level (or token/response-hybrid) objectives, while GSPO and GSPO-token use one response-level ratio. None of these objectives replaces token-count weights by normalized weights over labeled GUI/code action steps within a multi-action training sample.

Notation.

Let ii denote a training sample. Training sample ii contains KiK_{i} action steps. We denote by ai,ka_{i,k} the set of assistant-token positions that contribute to the loss for action step kk, and by |ai,k||a_{i,k}| its cardinality. Thus, ai,ka_{i,k} may include reasoning tokens, tool-format wrapper tokens, and action-content tokens. Let mi,t∈{0,1}m_{i,t}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether token position tt contributes to the loss. For each loss-participating assistant token, define the token-level importance weight and its logarithm as

wi,t​(θ)=πθ​(yi,t∣hi,t)πold​(yi,t∣hi,t),δi,t=log⁡wi,t​(θ)=log⁡πθ​(yi,t∣hi,t)−log⁡πold​(yi,t∣hi,t).w_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})}{\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})},\qquad\delta_{i,t}=\log w_{i,t}(\theta)=\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})-\log\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t}).

Here, yi,ty_{i,t} is the sampled token and hi,th_{i,t} is its preceding causal context. The total number of valid assistant tokens in sample ii is

Ni=∑tmi,t=∑k=1Ki|ai,k|.N_{i}=\sum_{t}m_{i,t}=\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}|a_{i,k}|.

For each action step, we define the mean token-level log-importance weight as

δ¯i,k=1|ai,k|​∑t∈ai,kδi,t.\bar{\delta}_{i,k}=\frac{1}{|a_{i,k}|}\sum_{t\in a_{i,k}}\delta_{i,t}.

Let τi,k\tau_{i,k} denote the action type of step kk, e.g., τi,k∈{GUI,code}\tau_{i,k}\in\{\mathrm{GUI},\mathrm{code}\}. We assign each action type a nonnegative balancing coefficient ατi,k\alpha_{\tau_{i,k}}. At least one action type in each sample must have a positive coefficient so that the normalizer below is nonzero.

E.1 GSPO

The standard GSPO sample-level importance ratio for sample ii is

wiGSPO​(θ)=exp⁡(1Ni​∑tmi,t​δi,t).w_{i}^{\mathrm{GSPO}}(\theta)=\exp\left(\frac{1}{N_{i}}\sum_{t}m_{i,t}\delta_{i,t}\right).

Grouping the loss-participating tokens by action step gives

log⁡wiGSPO​(θ)=∑k=1Ki|ai,k|Ni​δ¯i,k.\log w_{i}^{\mathrm{GSPO}}(\theta)=\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}\frac{|a_{i,k}|}{N_{i}}\bar{\delta}_{i,k}.

Therefore, in standard GSPO, the implicit weight of action step kk in the sample-level log-ratio is

ωi,kGSPO=|ai,k|∑j|ai,j|.\omega_{i,k}^{\mathrm{GSPO}}=\frac{|a_{i,k}|}{\sum_{j}|a_{i,j}|}.

This weight is determined by token count rather than by action semantics. If a sample contains two short GUI actions and one long code action, the code action can dominate log⁡wiGSPO​(θ)\log w_{i}^{\mathrm{GSPO}}(\theta) simply because it has more valid assistant tokens. The same ratio is then used for all tokens in the sample, so the long action also has disproportionate influence over whether the whole sample is clipped.

E.2 Step-Balanced GSPO

We replace token-count-based action weighting with explicit action-level weighting. Define

Zi=∑k=1Kiατi,k,ωi,k=ατi,kZi.Z_{i}=\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}\alpha_{\tau_{i,k}},\qquad\omega_{i,k}=\frac{\alpha_{\tau_{i,k}}}{Z_{i}}.

The step-balanced GSPO sample-level importance ratio is

wistep​(θ)=exp⁡(∑k=1Kiωi,k​δ¯i,k).\boxed{w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}(\theta)=\exp\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}\omega_{i,k}\bar{\delta}_{i,k}\right)}.

Equivalently, the ratio can be written directly in terms of policy log-probabilities as

wistep​(θ)=exp⁡[∑k=1Kiατi,k​(1|ai,k|​∑t∈ai,klog⁡πθ​(yi,t∣hi,t)πold​(yi,t∣hi,t))∑k=1Kiατi,k].\boxed{w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}(\theta)=\exp\left[\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}\alpha_{\tau_{i,k}}\left(\frac{1}{|a_{i,k}|}\sum_{t\in a_{i,k}}\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})}{\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})}\right)}{\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}\alpha_{\tau_{i,k}}}\right]}.

This formulation differs from standard GSPO only in the aggregation weights used to form the sample-level log-ratio. Standard GSPO weights each action step in proportion to its number of valid assistant tokens, whereas Step-balanced GSPO uses explicit action-level weights. When these weights are set proportional to token counts, the formulation recovers the original GSPO ratio as a special case.

The policy objective retains the standard GSPO structure. Given the sample-level advantage AiA_{i}, the unclipped objective is Ji​(θ)=Ai​wistep​(θ)J_{i}(\theta)=A_{i}w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}(\theta), and the clipped objective is

Jiclip​(θ)=min⁡(Ai​wistep​(θ),Ai​clip⁡(wistep​(θ),1−ϵlow,1+ϵhigh)).J_{i}^{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta)=\min\left(A_{i}w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}(\theta),A_{i}\operatorname{clip}\left(w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}(\theta),1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}\right)\right).

Any additional dual-clipping rule for negative advantages is applied in the same way as in standard GSPO, after replacing its sample-level ratio with wistep​(θ)w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}(\theta). In the reported experiments, the KL loss is disabled (Table 11), so the objective contains no additional token-level KL term. If a KL penalty is enabled in future variants, applying corresponding step-level weighting would avoid reintroducing token-count-dependent regularization. The per-sample training loss is Li​(θ)=−Jiclip​(θ)L_{i}(\theta)=-J_{i}^{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta), and the batch loss over BB samples is

L⁡(θ)=1B​∑i=1BLi​(θ).L(\theta)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}L_{i}(\theta).

E.3 Gradient Contribution

We now show that the proposed ratio removes the deterministic linear dependence between an action step’s aggregate scalar gradient coefficient and its token count. Consider the unclipped branch, where Li​(θ)=−Ai​wistep​(θ)L_{i}(\theta)=-A_{i}w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}(\theta). For any token t∈ai,kt\in a_{i,k}, only δ¯i,k\bar{\delta}_{i,k} depends on the corresponding current-policy log-probability. Therefore,

∂log⁡wistep​(θ)∂log⁡πθ​(yi,t∣hi,t)=ωi,k​1|ai,k|.\frac{\partial\log w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}(\theta)}{\partial\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})}=\omega_{i,k}\frac{1}{|a_{i,k}|}.

Since ∂wistep/∂log⁡wistep=wistep\partial w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}/\partial\log w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}=w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}, we have

∂Li∂log⁡πθ​(yi,t∣hi,t)=−Ai​wistep​(θ)​ωi,k|ai,k|.\frac{\partial L_{i}}{\partial\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})}=-A_{i}w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}(\theta)\frac{\omega_{i,k}}{|a_{i,k}|}.

Summing over all tokens in action step kk gives

∑t∈ai,k∂Li∂log⁡πθ​(yi,t∣hi,t)=−Ai​wistep​(θ)​ωi,k.\sum_{t\in a_{i,k}}\frac{\partial L_{i}}{\partial\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})}=-A_{i}w_{i}^{\mathrm{step}}(\theta)\omega_{i,k}.

Thus, the aggregate scalar coefficient of action step kk is independent of |ai,k||a_{i,k}|. This is the sense in which Step-balanced GSPO changes the optimization signal: it leaves the token-level importance weights wi,tw_{i,t} intact, but changes how their log values are aggregated into the sample-level importance ratio. Under standard GSPO, a long serialized action occupies a larger share of the sample-level log-ratio, so a successful code step can receive more aggregate scalar credit simply because it contains more assistant tokens. This does not mean that the routing token selecting the code tool is directly multiplied by the number of subsequent code tokens. Rather, the longer serialized action contributes more token-level gradient terms under the same sample-level advantage and can therefore exert disproportionate influence on the update direction. Step-balanced GSPO removes this deterministic length-based multiplier from the action-step aggregate coefficient, reinforcing a successful action as a step rather than in proportion to its serialized length. The full parameter gradient still depends on token-specific gradient directions, clipping activation, and reward correlations, so this analysis explains a source of token-length-driven drift toward code actions rather than providing a formal guarantee of correct modality routing.

Appendix F Case Study

This section presents two filtered synthesis tasks covering an office/code workflow and a media workflow. The first is grounded in a spreadsheet, whereas the second constructs and transfers persistent application configuration between a recording tool and a video editor. Together, they illustrate application–artifact composition, environment-grounded task specification, and component-wise terminal verification in executable task records. Both use reviewed rule-based evaluators that assign partial terminal credit across independently verifiable task components. We reproduce the task metadata, complete instructions, and selected rule code to make these success conditions concrete.

F.1 Synthesis Task Case Study 1: Office and Code Workflow

The first task spans LibreOffice Calc and VSCode. It starts from a spreadsheet containing vehicle records, requires row-level categorization in the spreadsheet, and then asks for a runnable Python audit script over the saved artifact. The task is labeled complex and estimated to require 30 interaction steps.

The evaluator averages three terminal checks. The first gives weighted credit for the header, correct per-row labels, and the absence of invalid labels. The second checks that the script reads an XLSX file and implements data-derived counting rather than only hard-coding an answer. The third runs the script and scores each category count independently before checking the strict output order and format.

This case illustrates component-wise terminal scoring for a workflow that crosses an office application and a code editor. The reward is assigned only after the episode, but it distinguishes spreadsheet correctness, the construction of a data-derived program, and the program’s executed output rather than collapsing those outcomes into a single pass–fail check.

F.2 Synthesis Task Case Study 2: Media Workflow

The second task connects OBS Studio and Shotcut. It configures a recording pipeline in OBS and then transfers the resulting resolution and frame-rate requirements to a compatible editing project in Shotcut. The task is labeled medium and estimated to require 22 interaction steps.

The evaluator averages configuration checks for the two applications and the final text record. OBS receives partial credit according to the number of correct recording-path, format, resolution, and frame-rate fields. Shotcut receives full credit for a matching 720p/30 project profile and partial credit when two of its three core fields match. The text record is scored independently by line.

This task has an explicit cross-application handoff: OBS establishes the recording specification, and Shotcut must instantiate a project that is compatible with it. The evaluator checks persistent application state and project metadata rather than replaying a prescribed action sequence, while the partial terminal score distinguishes incomplete configuration from a fully compatible production setup.

F.3 Agent Behavior Case Study: GUI–Code Coordination

Figure 6 shows two successful trajectories in which OS-Helix coordinates GUI perception with code execution. These cases are intended to make the learned hybrid behavior concrete: the GUI is used where the task depends on the current application state or a user-facing interface, while code is used where the same goal contains structured extraction, precise inspection, or repetitive operations.

In the first case, the agent starts from the browser/PDF interface and uses the opened course material to infer the lecture-file URL pattern. Once this pattern is grounded by GUI observation, the agent switches to code and downloads the remaining weekly PDFs in a loop. The important behavior is not simply that code is faster for downloading files, but that the code action is conditioned on information first obtained from the live GUI state. This illustrates a complementary route in which GUI interaction resolves task-specific context and code then executes the scalable part of the workflow.

In the second case, the agent inspects a payment spreadsheet with code to identify students whose tuition has not been paid, then returns to the GUI to fill the e-mail recipients in the mail client. Here, code provides reliable structured filtering over tabular records, while GUI interaction completes the user-facing communication step. Together, the two examples show that the unified action space allows the policy to decompose a task across modalities instead of committing to a single interface throughout the trajectory.

F.4 Agent Behavior Case Study: Cross-Modality Verification

Figure 7 presents two successful trajectories where one modality solves the task and the other verifies or repairs the result. This behavior is qualitatively different from merely choosing between GUI and code at the beginning of a task: the agent can use the second modality as an intermediate feedback channel, detect a mismatch between the intended and realized artifact, and then continue the trajectory with a corrective action.

In the spreadsheet-chart case, the agent first creates the requested clustered column chart with code. The subsequent GUI observation reveals that the produced chart only contains the Sales series and misses COGS, which would be difficult to notice from the code path alone without explicitly checking the rendered artifact. The agent then repairs the chart through code, producing the required two-series visualization. This trace shows how GUI feedback can expose visual or application-level errors in code-generated artifacts and turn them into actionable corrections.

In the slide-editing case, the agent performs the visible edits through GUI actions: it adds the note on the second slide and bolds the title. It then switches to code-based inspection of the saved presentation file to verify that the persistent artifact matches the instruction, including both the note text and the title formatting. This reverse direction, GUI for editing and code for validation, highlights that the benefit of the hybrid policy is bidirectional. Across the four successful traces in Appendix F.3 and Appendix F.4, the learned policy uses GUI and code as mutually checking and mutually enabling tools, supporting the claim that a unified GUI/code action space yields complementary problem solving rather than replacing one modality with the other.

F.5 Failure Analysis: Evaluation Coverage and Cross-Modality Handoffs

Figure 8 presents two representative failures that expose a gap between task specification and evaluation coverage, as well as a state-handoff problem at the GUI–code boundary. Rather than indicating a deficiency of either modality in isolation, these traces identify systematic challenges for a hybrid policy in interpreting visual intent and maintaining persistent state across modalities.

The top trace illustrates a specification–evaluation coverage gap. “Preserve the original formatting” defines a visual equivalence condition involving row banding, numeric display, borders, and other rendered attributes. When the instruction and validation signal do not fully characterize these attributes, or do not cover admissible solution paths equivalently, they create an underspecified proxy objective that can favor one modality. After code-based conversion, the agent detects a mismatch through the GUI but attributes it to missing currency symbols, adding dollar signs rather than restoring the missing alternating row shading. A natural GUI solution would select the Calc table and paste it into Writer, preserving its rendered appearance; serialization through code instead requires the visual formatting to be reconstructed explicitly. This case motivates aligning user intent, rendering semantics, and verification coverage so that the benchmark recognizes the full set of valid solutions without presupposing an action modality.

The bottom trace exposes a cross-modality state-handoff failure. The agent first completes the first subgoal correctly through the GUI. When code subsequently edits and saves the second subgoal, it writes only a local disk-side state and does not incorporate the preceding modification that remains in the GUI-resident state. The GUI then mistakes the code-side save for a global commit and selects “Don’t Save”, discarding the correct update for the first subgoal. This is not a planning failure on either subgoal in isolation; it is a loss of persistence and commit semantics at the modality transition. Reliable hybrid execution requires reconciling GUI-resident and code-side artifact states before handoff, while maintaining a consistent representation of save scope and commit status.

F.6 Trajectory Audit

We manually annotated 30 representative trajectories from the multi-step Work. category to examine whether modality transitions reflect task-grounded coordination. For each trajectory, we recorded the final outcome, a compressed flow of the key GUI and code stages involved in coordination, and the purpose of any state or information handoff. The reported flow retains the principal stages that produce, consume, verify, or repair the reported handoff, while omitting repeated within-modality actions and transitions unrelated to that handoff. As summarized in Table 17, 27/30 trajectories contain a grounded GUI/code handoff, including 22/30 in which one modality verifies or repairs state produced by the other. The audited set contains 21 successful, 4 partially successful, and 5 failed trajectories. In four of the five failed trajectories, cross-modal state is transferred correctly and failure arises later from task incompletion or application/tool errors. The remaining trajectory exposes a failed handoff: the PDF source observed in the GUI is replaced by a different, unverified URL when code writes the spreadsheet. As the audit covers only a representative task subset, the observed behavioral frequencies may not reflect the overall trends across the full benchmark. Moreover, the audited trajectories do not establish that the observed routing decisions are optimal. Even with these limitations, the examples directly show that OS-Helix performs task-grounded information handoffs and cross-modal verification and repair, using GUI and code as mutually enabling and checking mechanisms. This process-level evidence complements aggregate task scores, which capture outcomes rather than coordination behavior, and further supports our central claim that the model learns substantive cross-modal coordination.

Appendix G OS-Helix Tool Schema and Prompts

We report the prompts and tool schema used by OS-Helix for SFT, RL, and test-time inference, together with shortened generation and quality-review prompts used by the data infrastructure. The train prompt denotes the system prompt used during SFT, while RL and test-time inference use the inference prompt. The tool schema with code is shared across SFT, RL, and testing, and the action space follows the same schema. Prompts used to distill trajectories from different teacher models vary by teacher and are not enumerated here.

Decide whether\iow_now:NeΞrepair is required and give concise feedback for evaluator regeneration.\iow_now:NeΞ\iow_now:NeΞ# Review Dimensions\iow_now:NeΞ- Coverage: verify every critical condition in ‘instruction‘, ‘success˙criteria‘,\iow_now:NeΞ and ‘evaluation˙requirements˙text‘, including target identity, values, counts,\iow_now:NeΞ order, formatting, metadata, negative conditions, and any genuine dependency.\iow_now:NeΞ- Getter correctness: require concrete absolute VM paths consistent with the task.\iow_now:NeΞ A ‘vm˙file‘ result is a local cached file path that rule code must open or parse;\iow_now:NeΞ a ‘vm˙command˙line‘ result is stdout text.\iow_now:NeΞ- Structural validity: inspect the internal content or application-specific\iow_now:NeΞ structure that proves completion, rather than file existence or size alone.\iow_now:NeΞ- False-positive resistance: initial, empty, partial, stale, wrong-path, wrong-file,\iow_now:NeΞ or superficially similar states should receive low reward.\iow_now:NeΞ- Evidence matching: use deterministic rule checks when files or commands capture\iow_now:NeΞ the condition; use VLM evidence only for indispensable visual or unparsable state.\iow_now:NeΞ- Safety and determinism: avoid network access, package installation, destructive\iow_now:NeΞ commands, current external facts, and hidden assumptions.\iow_now:NeΞ\iow_now:NeΞ# Scoring and Repair\iow_now:NeΞUse integer scores from 1 (unusable) to 5 (excellent). Treat\iow_now:NeΞ‘evaluator˙quality˙score‘ as primary and use ‘coverage˙score‘,\iow_now:NeΞ‘getter˙correctness˙score‘, ‘structure˙validation˙score‘, and\iow_now:NeΞ‘false˙positive˙resistance˙score‘ to explain it. Set ‘repair˙required‘ to true\iow_now:NeΞwhenever schema/static validation or initial-state preflight failed, or whenever\iow_now:NeΞthe review finds a material quality defect. Name the missing check, incorrect\iow_now:NeΞgetter semantics, unsafe behavior, or false-positive path in ‘suggested˙repair‘.\iow_now:NeΞ\iow_now:NeΞ# Output\iow_now:NeΞReturn valid JSON only:\iow_now:NeΞ–\iow_now:NeΞ ”evaluator˙scores”: –\iow_now:NeΞ ”evaluator˙quality˙score”: 1,\iow_now:NeΞ ”coverage˙score”: 1,\iow_now:NeΞ ”getter˙correctness˙score”: 1,\iow_now:NeΞ ”structure˙validation˙score”: 1,\iow_now:NeΞ ”false˙positive˙resistance˙score”: 1\iow_now:NeΞ ˝,\iow_now:NeΞ ”rationale”: ”brief score rationale”,\iow_now:NeΞ ”repair˙required”: true,\iow_now:NeΞ ”rejected”: –\iow_now:NeΞ ”reason”: ”short˙reason”,\iow_now:NeΞ ”suggested˙repair”: ”concise actionable feedback”\iow_now:NeΞ ˝\iow_now:NeΞ˝

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
